content: The available evidence, based on limited data, suggests that there may be no significant effect of early complementary feeding (CF) introduction on length, weight, head circumference, and anemia among normal-term infants in lowand middle-income countries (LMICs) and high-income countries (HICs). One study provided iron-fortified complementary food to the intervention group, but no significant differences were observed in these outcomes among breastfed infants. A meta-analysis comparing the early introduction of CF (≤4 months of age) to introduction at 6 months of age among normal-term infants included 45 studies with 214,844 participants. The outcomes assessed included length/height, weight, and other growth parameters. However, the evidence remains uncertain for stunting, underweight, wasting, thinness, height/length, weight, head circumference, diarrhea, asthma, wheeze, eczema, rickets, respiratory illness, gastrointestinal illness, anemia, and iron deficiency anemia. None of the included studies reported on food preferences, non-communicable diseases (NCDs), or infant/child mortality. Subgroup analyses by country, based on limited data, showed no significant differences between HICs and LMICs. Similarly, no significant effects were observed between breastfed and formula-fed infants for height-for-age z-scores (HAZ), weight-for-age z-scores (WAZ), length, weight, body mass index (BMI), overweight, and obesity. Observational studies comparing early CF introduction (<6 months) to later introduction (≥6 months) included 45 studies with 214,844 participants. The findings suggest no significant effects on hemoglobin levels, serum ferritin, iron deficiency, or skinfold thickness. None of the included studies reported on bone mineral content (BMC), waist circumference, gut health/microbiome, or maternal outcomes. For late CF introduction (>6 months compared to ≤6 months), 22 studies with 95,779 participants were included. The evidence remains uncertain for stunting, underweight, wasting, thinness, overweight, obesity, asthma, wheeze, eczema, diarrhea, atopic dermatitis, food hypersensitivity, and anemia. None of the studies reported on HAZ, WAZ, developmental outcomes, food preferences, food allergies, NCDs, or infant/child mortality. Among preterm, small-for-gestational-age (SGA), or low-birth-weight (LBW) infants, three randomized controlled trials (RCTs) with 428 participants compared early CF introduction at 4 months to 6 months. The evidence remains uncertain for length, weight, severe anemia, weight-for-age z-scores (WAZ), acceptable minimum dietary diversity, minimum acceptable diet, diarrhea, lower respiratory tract infections (LRTI), sepsis, systolic blood pressure, diastolic blood pressure, and infant mortality. None of the studies reported on stunting, underweight, wasting, HAZ, weight-for-height z-scores (WHZ), food preferences, food allergies, or other NCDs. One RCT among preterm infants compared CF introduction at 3 months to 4 months and included 68 participants. The findings suggest no significant effects on hemoglobin, serum ferritin, or serum iron. None of the studies reported on BMC, waist circumference, skinfold thickness, gut health/microbiome, or maternal outcomes. In summary, the evidence regarding the timing of complementary feeding introduction remains inconclusive for most growth, health, and developmental outcomes across different populations, including normal-term, preterm, SGA, and LBW infants. Further high-quality research is needed to clarify these associations.
